name: Karl Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m from the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions or government, and your answers are confidential. What happens on a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 43 and manage three coordinators at the maintenance approvals desk of a large property company. I moved over from building service four months ago and have a bachelor’s degree, but I still need help with the approval rules and I am slower than the other managers. Our desk reads repair requests, checks contracts and books contractors; I miss walking a building before I decide what it needs. I have never used an AI tool.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband works full time in a college workshop, and our children are ten and fifteen. We have a mortgage but kept almost ten months of expenses saved from years when I worked evening callouts. The company pays me well, and there are plenty of property-management jobs nearby. I would rather keep steady work and pay than chase a promotion that sounds clever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the desk AI Plateau is a small filing change. A tenant with water through the ceiling still needs somebody to approve a repair before closing time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my own pay and hours would hold. We already have savings and two wages, though the mortgage and the children’s school costs remain real. I do not know why the company would need an AI tool for a problem the building caretaker could explain in one call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I would keep the morning call with caretakers and check large repair approvals against the contract book. If the company brings in a filing tool, I would ask the senior coordinator to show me where rejected requests go before I sign anything it sorts. We would continue the standing transfer to our mortgage reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the job. I dislike a new screen, but I am not worried about paying our bills in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did a caretaker catch this week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A leak report said “kitchen,” but the water was coming down from the flat above. The contractor would have brought the wrong part if we had only read the form. The caretaker climbed the stairs and called me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the filing tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would look at the rejected folder with the senior coordinator, but I would not run it myself until I understood the errors. I have managed without AI so far. I am not going to pretend comfort with it for a meeting.

say: **AI Plateau** changes filing, not the need to approve real repairs.
Caretakers should still **call** when a form hides the problem.
think: My **pay and hours** look steady with two household wages and savings.
I doubt an **AI filing tool** adds much to a caretaker’s direct report.
do: **Keep** morning caretaker calls and contract-book checks.
**Inspect** the rejected folder before signing off on any sorted requests.
feel: I feel **calm** about work and paying bills, despite disliking a new screen.
S0.quote: A tenant with water through the ceiling still needs somebody to approve a repair before closing time.
fieldNote: His **ten-month reserve**, two wages and many local jobs support calm in a mild scenario.
He has **never used AI** and wants a colleague to show errors before he trusts a filing tool.

steps.text: Keep morning caretaker calls and check large repairs against contracts
Continue the standing transfer into the household mortgage reserve

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the staff Steady Disruption could write repair replies, check contracts, book trades and answer tenants. Management should agree on workloads with employees before it calls those saved minutes a reason to cut people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At my desk, those are most of the tasks. I am still learning the manager job, so my post could be folded into another team. The reserve gives us time to search, but a family mortgage cannot live on savings forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I would record every approval where a caretaker’s visit changed the answer, then take those examples to our staff representative. If the company introduces a new system, I would ask for paid instruction from a coworker and use it only after I can check the mistakes. If my desk is cut after rollout, I would apply for the posted estate-service manager role only if its pay covers our mortgage and school costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about my post, although I do not expect to miss next month’s mortgage. I would rather know the real workload than hear that everything is efficient now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which example would you give the representative?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The leak where the form named the wrong room. I would show the original request, the caretaker’s call and the part actually fitted. That is work a neat booking count would hide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your husband support a different job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He would, if the pay and hours let us both cover the school week. Our older child can get home alone, but the ten-year-old cannot. We would compare the schedule before I accepted an offer.

say: **Repair automation** must come with agreed workloads, not hidden cuts.
Caretaker visits should count as **work**, not delays.
think: My new desk-manager post could be **combined** with another team.
The **reserve** buys a search, not endless mortgage payments.
do: **Record** approvals changed by caretaker visits during 2026.
**Ask** for paid coworker instruction before using a new system.
**Apply** for estate service if pay and school hours work.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a possible post cut, though the mortgage is covered now.
S1.quote: The reserve gives us time to search, but a family mortgage cannot live on savings forever.
fieldNote: He turns his **hands-on history** into examples for staff workload talks, while admitting his manager skill is still developing.
He will learn a **proven system** only with paid help from a coworker, not a solo experiment.

steps.text: Give caretaker-visit evidence to the staff representative for workload talks
Learn the new system with paid coworker instruction if introduced
Apply for estate-service vacancy only if pay and school hours fit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my team AGI by 2028 could handle the contracts, replies and bookings at our desk. The company owes people a written cut date and a fair chance at other work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Full thinking AI by 2028 could do most of my office job; robots doing hands-on building repairs arrive around 2031. I know the caretaker side, but the new manager title may not last. I expect the desk to shrink and think my own post might go, although ten months saved and other local firms give us choices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I would ask the staff representative to request a written cut timetable and severance terms, then talk with my husband about the mortgage and school timetable. In 2027 I would apply for two advertised building-service supervisor jobs only if they involve real site visits and pay enough to keep our household stable. If AGI arrives in 2028 and I lose the desk, I would take a confirmed site job rather than wait for this title to return.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious. Losing a well-paid job would hurt, but I have a trade background, savings and places to ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does a site job avoid AGI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not entirely. Its reports, ordering and rota could change in 2028 too; I would be applying for the building visits and contractor checks. Robots around 2031 may then change some physical tasks. I would not call a building-service job a shelter from AGI forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My husband and I would say I might work at different buildings, but their school and home are staying for now. We would wait for an offer before changing the family calendar. The ten-year-old worries when plans sound unfinished.

say: **AGI by 2028** calls for a written cut timetable and fair access to other posts.
I would not promise the desk-manager **title** survives.
think: Desk thinking work faces AGI in **2028**, before site robots around 2031.
My own post might go, but **savings and local firms** give choices.
do: **Request** cut dates and severance through the staff representative this month.
**Apply** in 2027 for site supervisor posts only with real visits and adequate pay.
**Take** a confirmed site offer after 2028 if my desk closes.
feel: I feel **anxious** about losing a well-paid post, with savings and alternatives.
S2.quote: I would not call a building-service job a shelter from AGI forever.
fieldNote: He understands **site reports** face thinking AI in 2028 and physical tasks may change after 2031.
His **reserve and local options** keep job risk serious but manageable.

steps.text: Ask staff representative to seek written cut dates and severance
Apply for building-service supervisor posts only with site visits and adequate pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say AGI by 2031 gives enough time to check which property roles are still needed on site. I would ask the staff representative to see actual vacancies and pay, not a list of course titles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My contract checking and booking could still go in 2031, with repair robots coming around 2034. A site supervisor still has reports and schedules that AGI could take in 2031, even if walking a damaged building stays human for a few more years. I have a choice of local firms, but not a guarantee of one particular opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In January 2027 I would ask the property director for a paid six-week return to site service, with cover for my desk and no reduction in salary, and take it if approved. I would use that trial to see whether my old inspection skill still fits the supervisor job. After 2031 I would apply for site work if a vacancy offers school-compatible hours and pay that covers our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the desk but less hurried. A real six-week trial tells me more than an online course I would resent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you look at during the six weeks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Roof leaks, lift complaints and the contractor notes that do not match what is on site. I would make a small record of where I still need help. I was a caretaker, but I have never supervised the whole estate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the director will not approve the trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my current post and ask for one paid site day when cover is available. I would not leave the three coordinators short without a manager. I could also ask a local firm about their posted supervisor duties.

say: **Five years** can fund a real site trial and show actual vacancies.
I would want **pay and hours**, not just course names.
think: Desk and site reports face **2031 AGI**, while repair robots follow around 2034.
Local employers offer choices, but a **specific vacancy** is uncertain.
do: **Take** a paid six-week site trial from January 2027 only with desk cover and full salary.
**Record** inspection skill gaps during the trial if approved.
**Apply** after 2031 only for site roles with mortgage pay and school hours.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about the desk, with time for a real trial.
S3.quote: I was a caretaker, but I have never supervised the whole estate.
fieldNote: He chooses a **six-week site trial** rather than repeating a course he does not trust.
The trial needs **desk cover** and full salary, while site paperwork remains exposed in 2031.
He says **uneasy**, but his desk post could go in 2031 before a site vacancy is certain.

steps.text: Take paid six-week site trial only with desk cover and full salary
Apply after 2031 for site roles only with mortgage pay and school-compatible hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say AGI by 2036 gives firms a decade to tell workers which jobs and wages remain. I would keep asking our staff representative for actual posts, not a promise that technology creates opportunities.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In ten years our children will be about twenty and twenty-five and we could have paid down more of the mortgage if both wages continue. My office approvals and a site supervisor’s reports still face thinking AI in 2036; robots for physical repair follow around 2039. I could leave management for a building-service role without moving the family if the pay is fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I would keep the caretaker call and the standing reserve transfer. I would check local site vacancies twice a year with the staff representative, and take a paid site posting before 2036 only if a firm offers one with the same pay. After AGI arrives in 2036, I would keep working in a site role if it still exists and fits our mortgage and the hours my husband and I can manage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the next few years. Ten years and a strong reserve give us room to choose without pretending the desk will last forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire early if the desk went?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I am 43 now, and even in ten years our mortgage may still be running. I want paid work I can do well. I would not spend the reserve to avoid learning the site job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your children see change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I take a site role soon, while our younger child is still at school, I might leave earlier for building visits and my husband would handle breakfast. By 2036 both children will be adults, so school routines will no longer decide the job. We would check a real rota before changing our hours.

say: A **decade** should bring real jobs, wages and staff input.
I would keep asking for **posted site roles**, not slogans.
think: Both wages could reduce the **mortgage** before 2036.
Office and site paperwork face **2036 AGI**, before repair robots around 2039.
do: **Keep** caretaker calls and the household reserve transfer in 2026.
**Review** local site vacancies twice a year with the staff representative.
**Take** an equal-pay site offer; stay after 2036 only if the role remains and pay and hours fit home.
feel: I feel **calm** about the next few years with time and savings.
S4.quote: I would not spend the reserve to avoid learning the site job.
fieldNote: He has **no wish to retire** and treats a real rota, equal pay and a firm offer as conditions.
His **long runway** and many local jobs make the next few years feel secure despite later AGI exposure.

steps.text: Keep morning caretaker calls and contract checks through 2026
Continue the standing transfer into mortgage reserve
Ask staff representative twice yearly for posted site jobs and wage terms
Take site posting only with equal pay and a firm offer

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the desk could close before I have found a site post with the right hours. A written timetable, severance and a paid trial back in building service would help. Our savings give us time, not a reason to accept any job.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who climbs the stairs when a tenant says the ceiling is wet. A report can say kitchen and still send a contractor to the wrong flat. I trust the person who has seen the leak.

headlineQuote: I trust the person who has seen the leak.
portrait: **Karl, 43**, recently moved from building service to a junior maintenance approvals manager at a large property company.
His **high pay**, two household wages, ten-month reserve and many local jobs protect a mortgage and two children.
He has **never used AI** and insists on a caretaker’s visit and contract book before approving repairs.
He is **calm** under AI Plateau, anxious about 2028 desk cuts, then seeks a paid site trial with pay and school-hour conditions.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could close his new desk before a suitable site post appears.
whatWouldHelp: A written **cut timetable**, severance and a paid site trial would help him choose.
